title: Synes, mene eller tro — opinions and beliefs
goal: Choose synes, mene, or tro for an evaluation, an opinion, or a belief about a situation.

objectives.statement: Choose synes, mene, or tro for an evaluation, an opinion, or a belief about a situation.

sections.title: A decision at the neighbourhood café

spans.value: Mina and Jonas help organize events at a small neighbourhood café in Trondheim. They are discussing whether the café should begin opening on Sundays. Mina has spoken to several customers, while Jonas has looked at staffing and costs.
Jeg synes det er hyggelig på kafeen på søndager.

blocks.translation: I think the café is pleasant on Sundays.

spans.value: Ja, men mener du at vi bør holde åpent hver søndag?

blocks.translation: Yes, but do you think we should open every Sunday?

spans.value: Jeg mener at vi bør prøve én søndag i måneden først.

blocks.translation: I think we should try one Sunday a month at first.

spans.value: Tror du mange kunder kommer?

blocks.translation: Do you think many customers will come?

spans.value: Ja, det tror jeg. Flere har spurt om søndagsåpent.

blocks.translation: Yes, I think so. Several people have asked about Sunday opening.

spans.value: Jeg er ikke så sikker. Jeg tror det blir rolig om vinteren.

blocks.translation: I’m not so sure. I think it will be quiet in winter.

spans.value: Kanskje. Men hva synes du om ideen generelt?

blocks.translation: Perhaps. But what do you think of the idea in general?

spans.value: Jeg synes ideen er god, men jeg mener at vi må undersøke kostnadene først.

blocks.translation: I think the idea is good, but I think we must examine the costs first.

spans.value: All three highlighted verbs can correspond to English
think
. Norwegian separates three kinds of thinking more clearly:

items.value: presents an evaluation or personal impression;
presents an opinion, viewpoint, or position;
presents a belief about what is true, likely, or possible.

spans.value: Jonas can therefore say that the idea seems good to him, argue that costs must be examined, and believe that winter Sundays will be quiet. These are related thoughts, but they are not the same kind of thought.
Use
synes
when you evaluate something or describe your personal impression of it. Common English translations include
think
find
, and sometimes
feel

no.value: Jeg synes kafeen er koselig.

en.value: I think the café is cosy.

no.value: Mina synes søndagsåpent er en god idé.

en.value: Mina thinks Sunday opening is a good idea.

no.value: Vi synes filmen var litt lang.

en.value: We thought the film was a little long.

no.value: Hva synes du om den nye menyen?

en.value: What do you think of the new menu?

spans.value: The speaker is not mainly claiming that something is objectively true. The speaker is evaluating it: pleasant, expensive, interesting, difficult, useful, boring, or good.
Compare two reactions to a concert:

no.value: Jeg synes konserten var fantastisk.

en.value: I thought the concert was fantastic.

spans.value: This is an evaluation of the concert.

no.value: Jeg tror konserten var utsolgt.

en.value: I think the concert was sold out.

spans.value: This is a belief about a fact. The speaker may not know whether every ticket was sold.
Checkpoint activity:
Read several short reactions to places, meals, films, courses, and events. Identify which sentences express a personal evaluation. Then restate those evaluations with
synes
. This belongs here because it isolates the most typical use of
synes
before other meanings of English
think
are introduced. A successful response would use
synes
for judgments such as pleasant, disappointing, practical, or difficult without treating them as uncertain facts.

sections.title: Mene: stating a viewpoint or position

spans.value: Use
mene
when you state what your opinion or position is, especially when the point could be discussed, defended, or acted on.

no.value: Jeg mener at kafeen bør holde åpent på søndager.

en.value: I think the café should open on Sundays.

no.value: Jonas mener at de må undersøke kostnadene først.

en.value: Jonas thinks they must examine the costs first.

no.value: Læreren mener at kurset trenger mer muntlig trening.

en.value: The teacher thinks the course needs more speaking practice.

no.value: Hva mener du om forslaget?

en.value: What is your opinion of the proposal?

spans.value: The opinions expressed with
mene
often concern what people should do, which solution is best, or how a situation ought to be understood.

no.value: Jeg mener at kommunen bør bygge flere sykkelveier.

en.value: I think the municipality should build more cycle paths.

no.value: Hun mener at møtet bør begynne tidligere.

en.value: She thinks the meeting should begin earlier.

no.value: Vi mener at denne løsningen er mest rettferdig.

en.value: We think this solution is the fairest.

spans.value: With
synes
, the speaker gives a personal assessment. With
mene
, the speaker takes a position.

no.value: Jeg synes den nye planen er komplisert.

en.value: I think the new plan is complicated.

no.value: Jeg mener at vi bør endre den nye planen.

en.value: I think we should change the new plan.

spans.value: The first sentence evaluates the plan. The second recommends a course of action.
The boundary is not always absolute. A speaker may use either
synes
or
mene
when giving a general opinion, but the emphasis changes:

no.value: Jeg synes forslaget er godt.

en.value: I think the proposal is good.

spans.value: The speaker evaluates the proposal positively.

no.value: Jeg mener at forslaget er den beste løsningen.

en.value: I think the proposal is the best solution.

spans.value: The speaker presents a considered position, perhaps as part of a discussion.
Checkpoint activity:
Return to Mina and Jonas’s meeting. Separate their personal reactions from their positions about what the café should do. Reformulate each position with
mene
. This activity follows the explanation of
mene
because the café discussion naturally contains both evaluations and recommendations. A successful response would distinguish liking the idea from arguing that the café should adopt a particular plan.
Use
tro
when you believe that something is true but do not present it as certain knowledge. It is also common for predictions and guesses.

no.value: Jeg tror mange kunder kommer på søndag.

en.value: I think many customers will come on Sunday.

no.value: Jonas tror det blir rolig om vinteren.

en.value: Jonas thinks it will be quiet in winter.

no.value: Jeg tror bussen er forsinket.

en.value: I think the bus is delayed.

no.value: Tror du hun er hjemme?

en.value: Do you think she is at home?

no.value: Vi tror møtet slutter klokka fire.

en.value: We think the meeting ends at four.

spans.value: These sentences concern facts or future situations that the speaker does not know for certain.
Compare an evaluation with a prediction:

no.value: Jeg synes søndager er fine.

en.value: I think Sundays are nice.

no.value: Jeg tror søndagen blir fin.

en.value: I think Sunday will be nice.

spans.value: The first sentence evaluates Sundays in general. The second predicts what a particular Sunday will be like.
Compare a position with a belief:

no.value: Jeg mener at vi bør ansette en ekstra person.

en.value: I think we should hire an additional person.

no.value: Jeg tror vi trenger en ekstra person.

en.value: I think we need an additional person.

spans.value: The first sentence gives a recommendation. The second presents the speaker’s belief about the staffing situation.
A useful short response is:

no.value: Kommer det mange kunder? – Ja, det tror jeg.

en.value: Will many customers come? – Yes, I think so.

no.value: Blir det dyrt? – Nei, det tror jeg ikke.

en.value: Will it be expensive? – No, I don’t think so.

spans.value: Here
det
refers back to the whole idea in the question.
Checkpoint activity:
Consider short situations in which information is incomplete: a late bus, tomorrow’s weather, attendance at an event, or the reason a colleague is absent. Express a reasonable belief using
tro
. This belongs here because uncertainty is the key contrast between
tro
and the other two verbs. A successful response would use
tro
for guesses and predictions rather than for personal ratings or recommendations.
The clearest way to understand the verbs is to apply all three to one topic.
Imagine a new library:

no.value: Jeg synes det nye biblioteket er lyst og rolig.

en.value: I think the new library is bright and quiet.

spans.value: This is the speaker’s impression.

no.value: Jeg mener at biblioteket bør være åpent lenger.

en.value: I think the library should stay open longer.

spans.value: This is the speaker’s position about opening hours.

no.value: Jeg tror mange studenter kommer til å bruke biblioteket om kvelden.

en.value: I think many students are going to use the library in the evening.

spans.value: This is a prediction.
Now imagine a language course:

no.value: Jeg synes kurset er nyttig.

en.value: I think the course is useful.

no.value: Jeg mener at vi bør ha mer tid til samtale.

en.value: I think we should have more time for conversation.

no.value: Jeg tror neste undervisningstime blir vanskelig.

en.value: I think the next class will be difficult.

spans.value: The topic stays the same, but the purpose changes: evaluation, position, then belief.
Contrast activity:
Work with one familiar situation, such as a course, workplace, local service, or planned journey. Produce three statements about it: a personal evaluation with
synes
, a position with
mene
, and an uncertain belief or prediction with
tro

. This checkpoint belongs here because it requires a deliberate three-way contrast while keeping the context stable. A successful response would show three different communicative purposes rather than three loosely interchangeable translations of English
think
The verb in a question helps show what kind of answer is expected.

no.value: Hva synes du om kafeen?

en.value: What do you think of the café?

spans.value: This usually asks for an evaluation: Is it pleasant, noisy, expensive, or attractive?

no.value: Hva mener du om søndagsåpent?

en.value: What is your opinion of Sunday opening?

spans.value: This asks for a viewpoint or position in a discussion.

no.value: Tror du kafeen får mange kunder på søndag?

en.value: Do you think the café will get many customers on Sunday?

spans.value: This asks whether the other person believes a situation is likely or true.
The answers should match the questions:

no.value: Hva synes du om lokalet? – Jeg synes det er koselig.

en.value: What do you think of the premises? – I think they are cosy.

no.value: Hva mener du om planen? – Jeg mener at vi bør prøve den i én måned.

en.value: What is your opinion of the plan? – I think we should try it for one month.

no.value: Tror du planen virker? – Ja, det tror jeg.

en.value: Do you think the plan will work? – Yes, I think so.

spans.value: Question-and-response activity:
Read short questions containing
synes
mene
, or
tro

, and give a response that matches the type of question. Use the café, a workplace meeting, and a community event as contexts. This belongs here because choosing the correct verb involves recognizing another speaker’s purpose as well as producing your own statement. A successful response would answer an evaluation with an evaluation, a viewpoint question with a position, and a belief question with a belief or prediction.
Using tro for every English use of think
English
think
often leads learners to choose
tro
too widely.

no.value: Jeg tror filmen er kjedelig.

en.value: I think the film is boring.

spans.value: This can be correct if the speaker has not seen the film and expects it to be boring.
If the speaker has watched the film and is evaluating it, use
synes

no.value: Jeg synes filmen er kjedelig.

en.value: I think the film is boring.

spans.value: Context decides whether
boring
is an uncertain expectation or a personal evaluation.
Using synes for a factual guess

no.value: Jeg synes møtet begynner klokka ni.

en.value: Incorrect for this meaning: I think the meeting starts at nine.

spans.value: This is normally unsuitable if the speaker is uncertain about the schedule. The intended meaning is a belief about a fact:

no.value: Jeg tror møtet begynner klokka ni.

en.value: I think the meeting starts at nine.

spans.value: Use
synes
only if the sentence genuinely expresses an evaluation.
Using tro for a recommendation

no.value: Jeg tror vi bør vente.

en.value: I think we should wait.

spans.value: This form may occur when the speaker presents the recommendation tentatively. However, when the purpose is to state a clear position in a discussion,
mene
is the more direct choice:

no.value: Jeg mener at vi bør vente.

en.value: I think we should wait.

spans.value: The difference is one of stance.
Tro
makes the thought sound more like a belief or tentative judgment;
mene
presents it as the speaker’s opinion.
Treating synes and mener as completely interchangeable
These verbs can overlap, but they highlight different things.

no.value: Jeg synes løsningen er upraktisk.

en.value: I think the solution is impractical.

spans.value: This evaluates the solution.

no.value: Jeg mener at vi trenger en annen løsning.

en.value: I think we need another solution.

spans.value: This states a position about what should happen.
A useful test is to ask yourself:

items.value: Am I reacting to or evaluating something? Use
Am I taking a position in a discussion? Use
Am I saying what I believe is true or likely? Use

spans.value: Mistake-identification activity:

Examine a statement in which the verb does not match the surrounding context, and select that verb. The feedback shows the fitting replacement and explains whether the context calls for an evaluation, a position, or a belief. This belongs here because learners must use context rather than translate
think
mechanically.
A week later, Mina and Jonas have checked the costs and spoken to the café staff.
Nå har jeg sett på tallene. Jeg tror vi får råd til å holde åpent én søndag i måneden.

blocks.translation: Now I’ve looked at the figures. I think we can afford to open one Sunday a month.

spans.value: Det var gode nyheter. Hva mener de ansatte?

blocks.translation: That was good news. What do the staff think?

spans.value: De mener at vi bør stenge litt tidligere på søndager.

blocks.translation: They think we should close a little earlier on Sundays.

spans.value: Det høres fornuftig ut. Jeg synes også at en kortere åpningsdag er bedre.

blocks.translation: That sounds sensible. I also think a shorter opening day is better.

spans.value: Tror du kundene blir fornøyde?

blocks.translation: Do you think the customers will be satisfied?

spans.value: Ja, det tror jeg. Og jeg synes dette er en god start.

blocks.translation: Yes, I think so. And I think this is a good start.

spans.value: The verbs continue to divide the work:

items.value: the café can afford the plan because he has formed a belief from the figures.
that the café should close earlier because they are stating a position.
a shorter day is better because she is evaluating the arrangement.
the customers will be satisfied because she is predicting their reaction.

spans.value: Context-completion activity:

Retell the café’s decision using the three verbs. Include the speakers’ evaluation of the plan, the staff’s position, and the prediction about customers. This belongs near the end because it returns to the chapter anchor and combines all three meanings in a coherent account. A successful response would choose verbs according to purpose while keeping Mina, Jonas, and the café decision logically consistent.
Without looking back, explain the three-way distinction in Norwegian. Then write one connected café update containing an evaluation with
synes
, an opinion or position with
mene
, and a belief or prediction with
tro
. A successful review response will make each verb’s purpose clear from context.

prompt.value: Use synes for a personal evaluation or impression. Use tro when the speaker is uncertain whether a fact is true. For example, Jeg synes kafeen er koselig. is an evaluation, while Jeg tror konserten var utsolgt. is a belief. Read these five reactions: 1. I think the café is cosy. 2. The meal was disappointing. 3. We thought the film was a little long. 4. I think the course is useful. 5. I think the concert was sold out. Answer in Norwegian. First label each item as evaluation or belief/fact. Then restate every evaluation in natural Bokmål with synes. Do not restate item 5 as a personal evaluation.

payload.judge_prompt: Check both the labels and the Norwegian restatements. Accept natural Bokmål variants that preserve each topic and evaluative meaning. Items 1–4 must be identified as evaluations and restated with synes; item 5 must be identified as a factual belief and not rewritten as an evaluation with synes.

criteria.instruction: Correctly identifies the personal evaluations and excludes the factual belief.
Restates every identified evaluation in natural Norwegian with synes and preserves its evaluative meaning.

prompt.value: Contrast Jeg synes den nye planen er komplisert. as a personal assessment with Jeg mener at vi bør endre den nye planen. as a position about what should happen. At Mina and Jonas's meeting, they discuss Sunday opening. Write two or three connected Norwegian sentences. Show Mina's personal reaction that Sunday opening is a good idea, and state Jonas's position that the café should stay open on Sundays. Use synes for the reaction and mener for the position. Make clear which sentence is a personal reaction and which is an argument about action.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Bokmål variants with the same roles and meanings. The response must separate Mina's personal evaluation from Jonas's position about what the café should do, use synes for the evaluation, and use mener for the action-oriented position.

criteria.instruction: Clearly distinguishes liking or evaluating the idea from arguing what the café should do.
Expresses the café action or recommendation with mener and preserves the Sunday-opening context.

prompt.value: Use Jeg tror bussen er forsinket. and Jeg tror søndagen blir fin. for uncertain facts and predictions. By contrast, Jeg synes søndager er fine. is a personal evaluation. Write one Norwegian sentence for each situation below. Use a form of tro for every sentence and express a reasonable belief, not a rating or recommendation. 1. The airport bus may be delayed. 2. Tomorrow's weather may be nice. 3. You do not know whether many people will attend a community event. 4. A colleague is absent, and you are unsure whether she is at home.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Bokmål variants with appropriate subjects, tense, and word order. Each sentence must use tror or another natural form of tro, preserve its situation, and express an uncertain fact or prediction rather than a personal evaluation or recommendation.

criteria.instruction: Uses tro in all four sentences and preserves each incomplete-information situation.
Expresses beliefs or predictions rather than synes evaluations or mene recommendations.

prompt.value: Keep one topic stable while changing the communicative purpose: personal impression, position about what should happen, and prediction about a future situation. Use one planned journey as your stable situation. Write three connected Norwegian sentences about it: - a personal evaluation with synes; - a position or recommendation with mener; - an uncertain belief or prediction with tror. Make the three purposes clearly different. Do not use three interchangeable translations of English think.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Bokmål wording about the same journey. Require one genuine evaluation with synes, one position or recommendation with mener, and one uncertain belief or prediction with tror. The three sentences must show distinct communicative purposes.

criteria.instruction: Produces one Norwegian statement with synes, one with mener, and one with tror.
Keeps one journey as the topic while clearly distinguishing evaluation, position, and belief or prediction.

prompt.value: A question with synes normally asks for an evaluation, a question with mener asks for a viewpoint or position, and a question with tror asks for a belief or prediction. Give one complete Norwegian reply to each question: 1. Café: Hva synes du om den nye menyen? 2. Workplace meeting: Hva mener du om den nye arbeidsplanen? 3. Community event: Tror du mange mennesker kommer på arrangementet? Match each reply to the purpose of its question: evaluation, position, or belief/prediction.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Norwegian replies with different but suitable content. The café reply must be an evaluation, the workplace reply must state a position or recommendation, and the event reply must express a belief or prediction. The replies must match the meanings signaled by synes, mener, and tror in the questions.

criteria.instruction: Answers the café question with a personal evaluation.
Answers the workplace question with a viewpoint or position about what should happen.
Answers the community-event question with a belief or prediction.

prompt.value: Distinguish a personal evaluation from an uncertain belief about a schedule. The speaker does not know the schedule and is stating a tentative belief, not evaluating the meeting. Select the one stance verb that does not fit this context in the sentence
Jeg synes møtet begynner klokka ni.

payload.feedback: Replace synes with tror. This sentence expresses an uncertain belief about a schedule, not a personal evaluation.

prompt.value: Use this café context: Jonas has checked the figures and believes they may afford to open one Sunday a month. The staff want to close somewhat earlier on Sundays. Mina evaluates a shorter opening day positively. They discuss whether customers will be satisfied. Retell the decision in four or five connected Norwegian sentences. Include: - Jonas's belief about affording one Sunday opening each month; - the staff's position that the café should close earlier on Sundays; - Mina's evaluation that a shorter opening day is better; - the prediction about whether customers will be satisfied. Use all three verbs according to their purposes: tro for belief or prediction, mene for the staff's position, and synes for Mina's evaluation. Keep Mina, Jonas, the staff, and the café decision logically consistent. Paraphrase rather than repeating the prompt verbatim.

payload.judge_prompt: Check all four required facts and their roles. Accept natural Bokmål paraphrases and pronoun choices, but require Jonas's affordability belief, the staff's earlier-closing position, Mina's evaluation of the shorter day, and the customer-satisfaction prediction. Require synes for the evaluation, mener for the position, and tro for beliefs or predictions, with a coherent café update.

criteria.instruction: Includes Jonas's belief that the café can afford one Sunday opening a month.
States the staff's position that the café should close earlier on Sundays with mener.
Presents Mina's evaluation that a shorter opening day is better with synes.
Includes a belief or prediction about customers being satisfied with tro.
Keeps the speakers, café decision, and relationships among the statements logically consistent.

prompt.value: Complete both parts in one response. Part A, in Norwegian, explain the three-way distinction among synes, mener, and tror. Part B, in Norwegian, write one connected café update containing an evaluation with synes, an opinion or position with mener, and a belief or prediction with tror. Make the context show why each verb is appropriate.

payload.judge_prompt: Check both parts. Part A must be in Norwegian and must distinguish personal evaluation, stated position, and uncertain belief or prediction. Part B must be a connected Norwegian café update with all three verbs used for those corresponding purposes. Accept varied natural wording that makes each purpose clear.

criteria.instruction: Explains in Norwegian that synes marks evaluation, mener marks a stated position, and tror marks uncertain belief or prediction.
Writes a connected Norwegian café update containing an evaluation with synes, a position with mener, and a belief or prediction with tror.
